We have in mind youngsters from age 15 or 16. The others are too young. So we hope they will be kept in school.
Mr. Speaker, I will conclude by stating that Canadians must work shoulder to shoulder and that with mutual trust, if we can forget the far-fetched and ludicrous suggestions heard from the Opposition benches, we as Canadians will all manage to live through these difficulties and enjoy once again the good life of yesteryear.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have to say to the Hon. Member for Montmorency-Orleans (Mr. Duclos) that I am surprised by his speech. I have always thought of him as being on the left-wing of the Liberal Party, but he sounded today like a real Conservative. The Hon. Member did some pretty judicious summarizing of the Conference Board report. This morning's The Globe and Mail reports the Conference Board as follows:

April 28, 1983
The Budget-Mr. Duclos
The Canadian economy should show steady improvement this year but there will be no major success in battling unemployment over the short term-
The article goes on to state that unemployment is now 12.8 per cent, that it will come down to 12.3 per cent this year and to 11.5 per cent next year. Why is it with unemployment over 12.5 per cent and with very high unemployment in his Province of Quebec-I suppose the highest of any Province in Canada except Newfoundland-that his Government will spend $1 billion a month to keep the Unemployment Insurance Fund solvent but can find less that $2 billion for job creation? Where is the sense in paying 1.5 million Canadian workers to sit at home doing nothing rather than putting them to work doing the kinds of useful things which the Hon. Member talked about?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This is the kind of language we have been used to, coming regularly as it does from people who know that they never will be in power. This is all so easy for people who can get 20, 30 or 12 Members elected at each general election and who have no sense of responsibilities. I explained why-maybe my hon. colleague was not listening, was sleeping, or whatever. But I explained that unemployment statistics are misleading since it is clear that with this economic recovery, there will be an increase in the labour force, and this means that instead of having 58 or 59 per cent-please correct me if I am wrong- but I know that in metropolitan Quebec City, there is possibly 58 per cent of all people between the ages of 15 and 64 on the labour market, whereas a normal rate might be 64 or 65 per cent. Clearly, Mr. Speaker, if you have people joining the labour force, at the unemployment statistics level, statistics that are based on the labour force, a reduction in the unemployment rate as such will not be as dramatic, as if the labour force were stable.
Now as concerns unemployment insurance, my view is that people drawing benefits are most respectable in the first place; they want to work but unfortunately the international situation is restricting this Government's room for manoeuvre, as in the case with every other Government, especially in the industrialized world.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I feel those points are not too easy to make, and I would invite my hon. colleague to visit us in Quebec during the next election. He will have a chance to express his views, and we will have a chance to answer, because it has been shown that Quebecers do trust the Liberal Party, and my belief is they will continue to do so, whatever the Hon. Member may say.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this budget's first priority is to help the private sector. Job creation and helping the consumer are not this budget's first priority. My question to the Member for Montmorency-Orleans (Mr. Duclos) is as follows: How can the Hon. Member support this budget, considering the large number of unemployed workers in this country, especially in the Province of Quebec?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am tempted to make the same preliminary remarks I made when answering the question put by the Member for Winnipeg-North (Mr. Orlikow). I fail to understand ... Perhaps the Hon. Member is not living in the same country or on the same planet. How can anyone see job creation and helping small- and medium-sized businesses as two opposing factors? I remember that some time ago at a meeting organized by a union local in Quebec City, I met a group of unemployed workers, and I remember entering a hall, and feeling the hostility. After talking to these people, I said: Let me say one thing. Maybe you will shout me down, but wait thirty seconds after I tell you what I am going to say now: The workers' best friend is a company that makes profits. I hope my hon. colleague agrees with me on that. Personally, I do not know any entrepreneurs or businessmen who would stay in business if they kept losing money, just to keep people working.
What I mean is that these are complementary measures, and that we have decided to create jobs across Canada by stimulating the private sector, by helping it to invest more readily, by creating favourable conditions, by creating a climate of confidence. That is certainly not contrary to a job creation policy. If my hon. colleague thinks that with a deficit of $40 or $45 billion and a Government that would take 70 or 75 per cent of the gross national product, we could perhaps do more, well, I wish he would look at what is happening in socialist countries, which I suppose he has had a chance to visit. He will see that State control of the entire economy and of all production factors does not bring prosperity.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member knows that in countries which have or have had social democratic Governments, such as Sweden, Norway and West Germany-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And France.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-and France, the rates of unemployment are much lower than that of Canada. In fact, Canada has the third highest rate of unemployment of all industrialized countries.
Does the Hon. Member not realize that the reason we have a large deficit is that such a high percentage of our labour force is unemployed? Does he not realize that when they are working they pay income taxes and have money to purchase goods on which the federal and provincial Governments receive sales tax and that companies make profits and pay corporation taxes? The Government has done nothing about unemployment. Since the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) took office it has increased every year. If we got the country working and people were employed, does the Hon. Member not agree that the large deficit would disappear?
[ Translation]

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am absolutely astonished at the Hon. Member's remarks. His examples are odd, to say the
April 28, 1983

least. He mentions the Social Democratic government in the Federal Republic of Germany. Germany, like other industrialized countries, also happens to be in a recession, and I would like to put the following question to the Hon. Member. Did Germany not have elections not long ago? Did the Christian Democrats not win that election? Was the Social Democratic Party not defeated? And is that how German voters showed their appreciation of Mr. Schmidt's social democratic government? The Hon. Member's example is somewhat inappropriate and, by the way, I referred briefly to this in my speech. We have the example of the economically disastrous policy of the French Socialist Government since May 1981. Canada is looking forward to an interesting, major and lasting economic recovery, while France is in a deep recession. No later than yesterday, there were demonstrations in Paris and demonstrations by farmers in the provinces. We have to be serious. To reply more specifically to the question asked by the Hon. Member, I shall simply tell him that we are doing exactly what he said to reduce the deficit, because with fiscal incentives to promote investment by the private sector, we shall be able to create jobs, which will mean more Canadians being employed, more tax revenue for the Federal Government and a gradual reduction of the deficit.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like many others before me, I would like to make a few comments on the budget speech delivered a few days ago. I was somewhat surprised to hear the Hon. Member for Montmorency-Orleans (Mr. Duclos) endorse so vigorously the administration of his Government. Like many others, I am convinced that he is very disappointed at what has been accomplished during the last fifteen years, and more particularly the last five years. The Hon. Member for Montmorency-Orleans is joking when he says that the youth employment incentive programs are not aimed at children of seven or eight, but 1 should remind him that his own Government is responsible for the mortgage of nearly $2,000 being imposed on every newborn child by our national debt. The Hon. Member forgot to mention it.
In any case, Mr. Speaker, I must recognize that the budget is an extremely important exercise in the administration of this country. It is difficult as well to give currency to the projections of the current Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) because over the past 15 years, since I first won a seat in the House, his predecessors have made umpteen projections which were all way off the mark. On the strength of projections based on unbelievably misleading factors and in light of the fact that for 15 years now the Government has been telling us that it will spur the economy and set the country back on the road to prosperity through increased spending, we have no choice but to admit that it has been quite the opposite. We ought to be very concerned indeed that history might repeat itself.
The Hon. Member for Montmorency-Orleans spoke about the catastrophic situation in certain countries of the world. I would suggest that Canadians are now in a catastrophic
The Budget-Mr. La Salle
situation for which this Government must assume full responsibility. It has taken the wrong decisions, it has failed to take action at the right time in vulnerable sectors and, therefore, it must bear the blame and the responsibility. For a number of years now we have been urging the Government to steer its economic policies so as to encourage the private sector to show economic leadership because it is much better at it than the Government. Someone said earlier that it was a matter of confidence. Of course it is a matter of confidence, and from confidence flows credibility.
Does the Minister of Finance now have the necessary credibility to inspire confidence in investors, businessmen and Canadians generally? We say no. We say no because he has demonstrated unparalleled hypocrisy when he took action and then afterwards heeded pleas from this side of the House to listen to the private sector and promote private investment. That same Minister, when he held the energy, mines and ressources portfolio, drove private industries right out of a leading sector in Canada, and that same Minister, the Minister of Finance, was responsible for Canada's loss of $30 to $40 billion in investments and about 150,000 to 250,000 direct and indirect jobs, particularly in that area. That Minister of Finance carries a lot of weight in Cabinet, a lot more than the Hon. Member for Montmorency-Orleans, we know that. Not so long ago, the Minister of Finance took a bit of a beating in the Gillespie affair, and he made a major blunder when he partly disclosed his budget, an issue on which the lid has been clamped. But still this was a tremendous blunder on the part of a senior minister. How can this same Minister of Finance, with so large a smile on budget night, have the credibility needed to lead the country to the prosperity he referred to in his budget or in his comments? No way, Mr. Speaker! In forsaking that trust, he lost the credibility needed to give Canadians the confidence that is so needed. And on top of that, we see, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) rushing in to cover him up on two incidents that called for an immediate resignation, if honour had had its way.
Those are the rules by which we are governed today. For those reasons, Mr. Speaker, I must recognize that the Government's current attempt to call upon the private sector, after having competed and fought with it, points first to unprecedented hypocrisy as I said, and, second, proves that we were right in enticing the private sector to do a better job than the state, which it can do. The Liberals are only now beginning to understand that.
How is it possible for us, Mr. Speaker, to accept the Government's invitation to put our trust in them in order to save the country? As we have seen these past 15 years, the more they are granted additional supplies, the bigger their deficits are getting. And the bigger the deficits, the heavier the cost of our
24946

April 28, 1983
The Budget-Mr. La Salle
national debt and the higher the unemployment rate. Certainly, the truth must be told in this House. I was literally shocked when I heard the Hon. Member for Montmorency-Orleans (Mr. Duclos) earlier today trying to defend this Government's unprecedented failure and incompetence. Such is the situation now, Mr. Speaker. Of course, they would not want us to say that in 1968, when I first came here, at the same time perhaps as the Hon. Member for Montmorency-Orleans, there were
358,000	unemployed, and the budget stood at a $12 billion. But in 1982, what a sad performance, Mr. Speaker, that is embarrassing for Liberal members and is reflected in this morning's Gallup polls. Of course, Mr. Speaker, the Liberals would rather not hear about it. They will tell the public at large that the race is not yet over. Indeed it is not, but Canadians are in an awful hurry to get this opportunity to say what they think of a Government that has been hurting them for too long. And I hope the message gets across: there were 358,000 unemployed in 1968, whereas we now have close to two millions. With a $12 billion budget! That is something Canadians understand. Now it is $100 billion. So they tell us: "We need money. We are going to straighten out the economy within the next 15 years." The budget has increased from $12 to $100 billion, the deficit has increased from $491 million in 1968 to $31 billion this year. The Minister of Finance with his usual big smile has told us in his budget that we are going to have $25 billion deficits over the next four years.
Despite a sad economic situation, those people are asking us to put our confidence in them although they are responsible for this country's unprecedented failure. That is the kind of administration we have, and now this is the kind of administration that we should condemn with all our energies just as we are now doing. Is there one businessman in this country who would have retained managers of that ilk in his business for more than six months? I do not think so, Mr. Speaker. Should Canadians also know that the national debt which amounted to $32 billion in 1968 has reached $160 billion this year? With such a record, the Government is seeking, with the investments which are provided for in this budget, and with the assurance that our economy is on the threshold of recovery-
Mr. Speaker, the Government is not telling the truth when it says that our economy is on the threshold of recovery, and when the Minister of Finance claims that unemployment will be maintained at its current level. Of course, our friends opposite will argue that newcomers will arrive on the labour market. But that was to be expected. If current statistics are good for the goose, they ought to be good for the gander too. The Government should have foreseen this, for they say that to govern is to foresee. The Government lacked both foresight and compassion in connection with the unemployment problem it had created. It was dishonest with the Canadian electorate by creating prosperity artificially, especially by going deeply into debt over the past 15 years. And it succeeded during the last election campaign in convincing a majority of Canadians
that things were not so bad, since it was able to spend huge amounts of money and create social programs. Unfortunately, it started to compete with the private sector, the major provider of jobs, and now it is seeking its forgiveness.
We cannot forgive the Government for its poor performance. We cannot forgive the Government for wanting to compete on a daily basis with the provinces and the private sector, by setting unilateral guidelines. It is unthinkable. Good times are over for this Government. It has never felt the need to sit down with the business sector, the unions or the provinces and to behave as a good federalist should, respectful of the provinces, its partners, and to discuss national issues with them. That is the kind of administration we have had for the past 15 years. And it is not seeking the people's confidence. I suggest it is going too far, Mr. Speaker. It has waited too long. It will be judged on its actions. It is responsible for an impossible situation. Earlier, I heard an Hon. Member refer to the great strides made by the housing industry towards recovery. This Government is responsible, Mr. Speaker, because its lack of housing policy during the past three years, for the loss of
500,000	jobs in the construction industry. Today, I support the $3,000 grant for the purchase of a new home, but the Minister is not even in a position to state a specific date and this is disturbing and I think that the Government Members will realize the importance of the matter. The Minister said in his budget speech that the grant could be extended until the end of May. You can see what will happen, Mr. Speaker. Applications will be filed, but because the funds will have already been expended, the applicants will not be entitled to their $3,000. What is the exact date? The Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) said that the $3,000 grants could be extended until the end of May. However, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) is not convinced. Let us look at the budget. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) is not really sure of that. Then let us imagine for a moment what people will... Surely that-

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You did say 500,000 jobs!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs is not sure that 500,000 jobs will be lost but there are now some two million unemployed so I think that he should also check his statistics again.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I think that such an irresponsible Minister is wrong when he does not provide for the termination date for the $3,000 grants. I urge the Minister of Finance to tell Canadians that they will be entitled to the grants up to a specific date and if it is May 31, that will be fine, but any application filed within that period should be accepted. If the Minister of Finance fears that the Government cannot promise to pay that $3,000 grant to new owners, he should be brave and honest enough to say so. I ask him to give us a specific date, to set a specific time.
April 28, 1983

Mr. Speaker, I should end now considering the time allotted to me but before doing so I should like to mention that this Government has lost public confidence as is evidenced by public opinion polls. This Government is responsible for the problems which Canadians are now experiencing and is asking us to support proposals which it never made. However, through the force of circumstances, because it was forced to act, because we demanded that the private sector be used in a certain way, it does no longer deserve our support and should be dumped as quickly as possible.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO STIMULATE PURCHASES OF DURABLE GOODS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, there is a provision in the budget speech of April 19 which has not yet received all the attention it really deserves, for it will benefit Canadian families. Indeed, under that provision, Canadian taxpayers will be permitted to withdraw tax free part or all of their accumulated savings in RHOSP's, that is Registered Homeownership Savings Plans, provided such funds are used to purchase home furnishings and appliances before the end of 1983. They will not be required to close the plan for such withdrawals. Qualifying new home furnishings must generally be purchased between the date of the budget and December 31, 1983. That measure should stimulate consumer expenditures on durable goods. Thus, young couples will participate in the economic recovery. Through the purchase of furniture, refrigerators, washing machines or carpeting, they will contribute to inventory reduction and production of the manufacturing industry. Furthermore I think that mention should be made of that measure and, at the same time, those responsible for it, should be praised.

subtopic: COVERAGE OF FARM WORKERS-EFFECT ON EMPLOYERS
COVERAGE OF FARM WORKERS-EFFECT ON EMPLOYERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am extremely concerned about the revocation of Regulation 16
of the Unemployment Insurance Act. Not only are farmers being burdened with the additional difficulties encountered with the administrative obligation, coupled with high turnover and mobility of agricultural workers, but now, to add insult to injury, the federal Government, with its bureaucratic red tape and usual slowness, has not even made available the proper forms which it is forcing our farmers to use.
In my constituency the farmers of Haldimand-Norfolk will need at least 50,000 forms by June 10 when the 1983 strawberry harvest begins. That is less than eight weeks away. One farmer alone will need at least 2,000 forms by that date. The present forms, as I am sure the Minister knows, are only valid until April 30. That means the only forms available will be out of date for this season.
The new program requires filling out a daily form for each individual worker, complete with Social Insurance Number and other pertinent detailed information. This is a horrendous, time consuming, impossible task for farmers to perform at the eight of the season, especially when dealing with crops such as strawberries. Many farmers employ up to 400 seasonal workers per day.
I understand the Minister is reconsidering this stand and is meeting with the horticultural society this week. I urge the Minister to listen carefully to this group and to take immediate steps to offer some sort of relief to our frustrated farmers.

subtopic: COVERAGE OF FARM WORKERS-EFFECT ON EMPLOYERS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

Madam Speaker, it is no secret that agriculture as an industry is suffering along with many other sectors of Canada's economy. An Act that the Government could use to alleviate somewhat the problems in agriculture, particularly western agriculture, is the Western Grain Stabilization Act. That Act has been in place since 1976, and in the seven years since its inception has had a pay out twice, once in 1977 and once in 1978. Currently the fund has in excess of $600 million, and at the present rate of contribution there will be in excess of $800 million in the fund at the end of this year.
The Act is jointly funded by the producers and the federal Government on the basis of $2 of contribution by the federal Government for every $1 of contribution by producers. The producers' contribution is collected on the basis of 2 per cent of eligible grain sales.

April 28, 1983
24948___________________________
The Act is designed to stabilize net farm income over a period of five years. If the Government chose to do so, it could amend the Act so that it would stabilize income over a three-year period rather than a five-year period. If that amendment were made, there would be a payment triggered immediately of something approximating $150 million. That money would be injected into the western farm economy. It would be good for the economy and would not increase the deficit one bit. It would be a step that the Government could take to assist the agricultural industry at a time when it needs help, without increasing the Government's deficit.

Madam Speaker, the appointment of Madam Justice Constance Glube as Chief Justice of the Nova Scotia Supreme Court Trial Division is welcome news, though perhaps not for our friends in labour, as it is the elevation of a distinguished member of the Nova Scotia bench and she is the first woman to be appointed as a Chief Justice in Canada.
The appointment of women to the bench is of ever greater importance now that we have an entrenched Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Because of the Charter the judiciary will influence our lives much more than it has in the past.
Strong representation of women on the bench, indeed equal representation, was a demand of Canadian women's organizations in the Charter debate. Yet the proportion of women appointed to the bench over the last three years has been only 8.9 per cent, the very same as the proportion of women appointed to the bench in the United States by President Reagan, one whose leadership in the feminist cause is hardly to be emulated.
Some extremely bad decisions of the Supreme Court of Canada recently underscored the need to appoint men and women with sensitivity to women's issues. The Leatherdale case of last year repeats some of the horrors of the Murdoch case of ten years ago. Only yesterday a decision was announced which would put the victim of rape on trial for conduct after the offence, a possibility that would never be considered for victims of any other offence. It is time that sensitivity and competence on women's issues become criteria for the selection of members of the bench in Canada.
Hear, hear!

maintopic: CALL FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF NON-DIPLOMATIC PRESENCE IN TAIWAN
CALL FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF NON-DIPLOMATIC PRESENCE IN TAIWAN
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, unemployment is our number one problem today and international trade plays an important part in that problem. For every $1 billion spent on trade, approximately 25,000 new Canadian jobs are created.
Unlike most other countries, however, Canada has not reached its full potential in this regard. For example, one of the fastest growing economies in the world is Taiwan, and although not recognized diplomatically by many nations, virtually all non-communist countries have established some form of bilateral non-diplomatic presence with Taiwan for the sake of promoting trade.
I am pleased to announce today that members of the Cana-da-Taiwan Parliamentary Friendship Committee, consisting of some 50 Members of Parliament from both sides of the House, have received assurances in writing from the Minster of Foreign Affairs in Taiwan that serious consideration is being given to sending a procurement mission to Canada in the near future in order to buy Canadian goods and services. This, we believe, is only a small step toward utilizing the full trade potential between Canada and Taiwan, a potential that would create tens of thousands of jobs in Canada forthwith.
To this end we urge the Government to join virtually all other non-communist industrialized nations in establishing a non-diplomatic presence in Taiwan in order to take full advantage of the tremendous trade potential for the benefit of all Canadians.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

Madam Speaker, yesterday President Reagan addressed the combined Houses of the Senate and the Congress of the United States. He asked for more arms for the struggles in Central America. On the same day, Dr. Alfred Gelhorn of the Harvard School of Public Health, and three other U.S. professionals, tabled a report about their visit to El Salvador in recent months. They wrote:
The rate of endemic diseases is rising drastically as social programs are sacrificed so that funds can be allocated to the military.
They went on to say:
U.S. foreign aid must make abundant provisions for such essentials as food, medicine, vaccines, medical equipment, teaching materials for students, and other forms of economic assistance.
Furthermore, they said:
Wherever we turned we found the chilling effects of the ever-widening devastation to health and health care that has been caused by the breakdown in
April 28, 1983

education, the slashing of budgets for national health programs and the repression of human beings by the systematic use of terror.
The doctors went on to say that they had visited a hospital. Ten days after their visit, a doctor had been taken from that clinic by armed men and has not been seen again.
I would ask the Senators and Congressmen of the United States to check their facts carefully. They must realize that the United States was founded in 1776 by a group of people who were able to identify oppression. I believe that if George Washington and Benjamin Franklin were alive today, they would be on the side of the revolutionaries.
Hear, hear!

maintopic: FIFTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF 4-H CLUBS TRIBUTE TO ACCOMPLISHMENTS
FIFTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF 4-H CLUBS TRIBUTE TO ACCOMPLISHMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the 4-H organization has made Canada a better country. The first meetings of 4-H were held some 70 years ago. In 1933, under the Dominion Companies Act, 4-H was incorporated as a nonprofit youth organization. Canada now has more than 5,500 clubs, with some 75,000 members who complete about 80,000 projects every year.
Every 4-H-er pledges the head for clearer thinking, the heart for greater loyalty and understanding, the hands for larger service, and health for a better and more worth-while life. Members learn to do by doing under the guidance of volunteer leaders who encourage special interests in agriculture and in living and in identifying leadership ability in the members of the club and in themselves.
The basic objective of this educational movement for young people is to provide a well balanced training in citizenship and to encourage the adoption of improved methods in farming and in homemaking. Fifty golden years of service, plus 20 years before incorporation in Canada, together with youth and leaders in some 80 countries of the world, building character by the four "H's", the "Head", "Heart", "Hand" and "Health", have had a tremendous impact for good throughout the world. I am sure every Hon. Member of this House will join with me in saying "Congratulations" and thanks to the 4-H Movement.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CALL FOR SUPPORT OF CANADIAN INDUSTRY
CALL FOR SUPPORT OF CANADIAN INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Canadians know that any
economic recovery in this country will be led by the business community. The textile industry, which employs 13 per cent of the people in the manufacturing sector, continually finds that it must struggle with unfair foreign competition, and if this is allowed to continue it will seriously jeopardize the textile industry's more than 80,000 employees and add to the already two million Canadians who are out of work.
On behalf of the over 1,100 textile workers and their families who live in the federal constituency of Hastings-Fron-tenac-Lennox and Addington, as well as the other thousands of Canadians and their families who are currently employed in the textile industry, I ask that the responsible Minister and his Government support the Canadian domestic market. Canada cannot be allowed to sink gradually deeper and deeper into foreign control of our domestic market.
Canadians must provide for Canadians so that we are in the driver's seat for our future, and the Government must help us drive forward, not backward. I ask the Government to show the understanding and co-operation which will support and encourage industry to grow for the future, and thus prevent loss of jobs in Canada.

maintopic: PETRO-CANADA SELLING TIRES IN COMPETITION WITH INDEPENDENT DEALERS
PETRO-CANADA SELLING TIRES IN COMPETITION WITH INDEPENDENT DEALERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to raise a matter which has been brought to my attention by the Atlantic Provinces Tire Dealers and Retreaders Association which represents approximately 30 tire dealers in the Atlantic Provinces. These dealers employ over 1,000 people and have built up their businesses over a number of years with private funds. They are deeply concerned over the fact that Petro-Canada Tire Centres are offering ridiculously low tire prices which make for extremely tough competition.
These privately owned businesses would like to question the Government's responsibility to the public when it has gotten into the business of selling tires as a Crown Corporation in competition with tax-paying businesses which have built up reputations in their local communities. The Government also pays out large sums of money to advertise special prices for huge sales of tires in full-page $1,000 advertisements, using taxpayers' money.
It is extremely difficult for business people to stay in business and make a profit in today's harsh economy, let alone compete with a company using subsidized tax dollars. I, on behalf of the Atlantic Provinces Tire Dealers and Retreaders Association, urge that an immediate halt to such business methods, at the cost of over-burdened taxpayers across the country, take place, and that the Government be held responsible for the detrimental effect this practice is having on our business sector.

April 28, 1983
Oral Questions HEALTH

Madam Speaker, the House will be aware that as a result of the application of the six and five program to the funding for the Medical Research Council, only 12 per cent of the new applications for research funding which were made this year to the Medical Research Council were approved. This is the result of this cutback in funding.
The concern is that we may be sending the wrong message to young people who are studying in our universities in order to do important research. We may, perhaps, be sending them the message that they would have been better to go into land speculation because the Government does not have the right sense of priorities if it applies the six and five program to medical research. Government will create a sort of lost generation of young people for work in scientific research if it does not smarten up pretty soon and start making medical research a priority, instead of relying on devious and dubious means like the proposed sports pool for the funding of health research.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister responsible for the Special Recovery Program, and it relates to the disbursement of funds under this Program to the various regions of Canada. Bearing in mind that the unemployment rate in British Columbia has reached an all-time high, and one of the highest in Canada, will the Minister confirm for this House that some $400 million of funding under the Special Recovery Program is being allocated to British Columbia? subsubtopic: INQUIRY RESPECTING ALLOCATION OF FUNDS TO BRITISH COLUMBIA

subsubtopic: ACHIEVEMENT OF FULL EMPLOYMENT-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:

This follows the Minister of Finance's rather bizarre notion, as expressed last week, that 8 per cent or 9 per cent unemployment should really constitute full employment. Instead of dealing with the problem, the Government is really redefining the issue.
Considering that an all-Party Committee of this House, following the last election, recommended to the Government that it accept a level no higher than 4 per cent as the definition of full employment, why does the Government not accept this definition and then set targets to achieve it?

speechtext: Madam Speaker, considering that certain countries in the world today have unemployment of 4 per cent or less-Austria, Sweden, and Japan, to name three-and considering that is because they have had political leadership which set that level as a target, why will the Minister not now answer the question I put to him in the first place and accept as a minimum target a level of unemployment of 4 per cent for this country?

speechtext: Madam Speaker, it is interesting that the Hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party points to countries such as Austria and Japan as examples. speechtext:

April 28, 1983

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: VISIT BY INVESTIGATORS TO TORONTO NEWSPAPER OFFICE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I did not call the RCMP at all. I think there is some internal procedure in every Department to deal with people who give information which should not be given outside. If there is an inquiry, it is through the normal process of the Department, and I have not even been consulted about it.

Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the Solicitor General, who has responsibility in the House for the RCMP. The Minister may call on the police, or any citizen may call on them, when wrongdoing is suspected, but the suggestion that they are being used by the Government is totally unjustified.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Finance my question is directed to the Minister of State for Finance. speechtext:

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF BUDGET PROVISIONS-CONFERENCE BOARD FORECAST
speechtext:

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul J. Cosgrove (Minister of State (Finance)):
subsubtopic: EFFECT OF BUDGET PROVISIONS-CONFERENCE BOARD FORECAST
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have not had an opportunity of reading the report to which the Hon. Member has referred. She has indicated that she, herself, heard a news report by Mr. Maxwell. I similarly heard reports, and we must have heard different radio reports because the one which I heard, on the contrary, did not at all confirm the protestations of the Hon. Member.
The report of the Conference Board is at best neutral concerning the design of the budget, which is to add a stimulus to an economy which is presently growing and showing some strength, with a plan to support the economy immediately, through the next year and some months, and then to recoup those moneys added as a stimulus by way of taxation at a later date when it could be afforded by the private sector. That basic premise was not the subject of the report of the Conference Board. Indeed, if it had been, it would have been a prerelease of the budget which the Minister introduced Tuesday last.
Therefore, in reply to the Hon. Member's affirmation that the Conference Board criticized the strategy of the Minister of Finance, of adding stimulus at this time, but in a responsible way, putting a plan forward which would call for a reduction of the deficit at a time when the economy was strengthened, I suggest that that statement was not criticized by the Conference report, and the Hon. Mr. Maxwell stated in his interview, "I think we are very much in line with what most people are saying". Do these assessments disturb the Minister? Is the Goverment having sober second thoughts?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul J. Cosgrove (Minister of State (Finance)):
speechtext:
Not
at all, Madam Speaker. We believe, for example, that the stock market has responded favourably to the strategy of the
Government, of the Minister of Finance, that is, of moderate stimulus at this time. However, with the concern about a reduction in the long-term deficit, we think that that is why there has been an improvement on the stock market. We think that is why the budget has been well received on the international financial markets and why the Canadian dollar has strengthened. We believe that the strategy has been supported by the majority of writers, critics and economists who have studied it. Yes, of course, there are differences of opinion. There always will be. However, they are in a minority, just as is the Hon. Member.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. Canada's special ownership charge on oil was ostensibly placed to pay for the purchase of Petrofina. It has not been rescinded in the recent budget. The Gallup Poll shows that some 69 per cent of Canadians make absolutely no effort to buy their gasoline at Petro-Canada stations and 45 per cent think that the Crown corporation should be sold. Will the Minister tell the House that the Government is now willing to accept the fact that this is a costly and obviously unpopular burden to the taxpayer?

subsubtopic: MR. NIELSEN-ALLEGED UNAUTHORISED INTRUSION INTO OFFICES OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION-RULING BY MADAM SPEAKER
speechtext:
I would like today to rule on the question of privilege raised by the Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. April 28, 1983

Nielsen) concerning the removal from his office of certain carvings. The Hon. Leader of the Opposition was good enough to write to me on April 22 and draw my attention to a ruling given by Speaker Lamoureux on September 4, 1973 in relation to another case, as he did allude to it in the course of his presentation.
I have made an investigation, as I promised, into the matter and ascertained that the carvings were in fact removed by officials of the Department of Public Works from the conference room of the Leader of the Opposition just next to his office. They were removed in order that certain work which had been authorized could be carried out. Nevertheless, the Department should have contacted the Sergeant-at-Arms to seek his permission before doing so. The fact that they did not do so is regrettable, and I apologize to the Hon. Leader of the Opposition. But I am satisfied that it was an honest oversight and was not done with any questionable intention. No break-in occurred and the employees were accompanied by a security guard when the carvings were removed.
The purpose of removing the carvings was to comply with our bilingualism policy-

subsubtopic: MR. NIELSEN-ALLEGED UNAUTHORISED INTRUSION INTO OFFICES OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION-RULING BY MADAM SPEAKER
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. NIELSEN-ALLEGED UNAUTHORISED INTRUSION INTO OFFICES OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION-RULING BY MADAM SPEAKER
speechtext:
Members are not in favour of that? The purpose was to translate the postings and inscriptions so that they should appear in both languages. However, upon examination of that particular case it became obvious to me that it would not be proper to attempt a translation of these particular inscriptions which turn out to be part of our anecdotal history. They should be left as they are. 1 have ordered that the carvings be replaced in the conference room. They were removed on a Monday; the matter was raised on a Thursday, and they are now in place as of yesterday morning at eight o'clock, I might add with the full permission of the Hon. Leader of the Opposition.
There is no doubt that unauthorized entry into the office of a Member of Parliament can constitute a breach of privilege and a break-in would certainly do so. There are precedents to this effect. However, the precedent quoted by the Hon. Leader of the Opposition in his letter to me and in his presentation did not really involve unauthorized entry. In that case police officers entered a Member's office and questioned her staff without having first sought permission from the Speaker to do so. The offence lay in the actual interrogation of the staff, not in the entry into the Member's office. This was ruled by my predecessor to be "an apparent breach of a Member's privilege", even though no actual break-in was involved.
On the matter of entering Members' offices, it is important to distinguish between unauthorized entry for a nefarious purpose and entry for a legitimate reason. I refer Hon. Members to the fact that if a fire broke out in a Member's office, someone would obviously have to enter it. Cleaning personnel and security enter Members' offices, but of course these two particular instances are understood and accepted.
In the case of which the Hon. Leader of the Opposition complained there was no break-in, although it is acknowledged
Privilege-Mr. Nielsen
that the officials concerned should first have sought the permission of the Hon. Leader of the Opposition before removing the carvings. The circumstances of the entry were not consistent with anything which could constitute a contempt of Parliament or a breach of the Hon. Member's privilege. Therefore I rule that there is no question of privilege, but I thank the Hon. Member for having raised the matter.

I am as concerned as the Minister of Public Works (Mr. LeBlanc) will be, whose responsibility it is for the maintenance of these buildings, about changes which are occurring without the knowledge of Hon. Surely these decisions should be made in consultation with Members of the House, because alterations to these buildings or premises are the direct concern of all Hon. Members of the House. I would like to have the assurance of the Chair that it will examine the feasibility of requesting the House leaders to consult their caucuses in regard to setting up such an all-Party committee for the purpose of consultation and to work with whatever other machinery may be in place so that we achieve not only the letter but the spirit of the law of the Official Languages Act and at the same time keep within the determination to preserve the heritage nature of these buildings.

subsubtopic: MR. NIELSEN-ALLEGED UNAUTHORISED INTRUSION INTO OFFICES OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION-RULING BY MADAM SPEAKER
speechtext:
The Hon. Member just rose, I guess; he was asking a question which I am pleased to answer. I reassure the Hon. Leader of the Opposition that some of the inscriptions, such as the one he just mentioned, "Dieu le veut", "Honour the King" and others should not be translated and cannot be translated in any circumstance. In this particular case there was a divergence of opinion among committee members who had to deal with the matter and somehow instructions were given to deal with the inscriptions in the conference room. Having myself examined them, as I said in my ruling I feel the particular expressions should not be translated.
As for the broader matter of who gave the instructions, the initiative to have the law on bilingualism apply to the House of Commons is, of course, left to the Speaker. Obviously the Department of Public Works, which looks after the physical aspects of the House of Commons buildings, would not act except on instructions or a request from the Speaker. That is exactly the procedure which was followed. Advice was sought from experts such as architects in all cases where it was thought the postings should be bilingual. I think this was done, if I may express an opinion, in the best of taste because we did require the advice of those who are knowledgeable in these matters.
As for the matter of consultations which the Hon. Member touched upon, I must say that it is very difficult for the Speaker to administer the budget of the House of Commons, which is quite considerable, $141 million, through constant consultations. At some point the Speaker consults because the Speaker feels there is a controversial matter that will in some way disturb some Members. Therefore the Speaker does have consultations. In general, that is my approach.
Sometimes I do proceed without informing a committee or consulting caucus because I interpret it as being my responsibility and administrative duty to proceed. There was a committee set up, not of Members of all Parties, but all of those who have a responsibility for the physical buildings in which we carry out our function. It is a matter of choice as to when to form a committee and when not to proceed in that fashion. Hon. Members must understand that I cannot constantly be forming committees to proceed with most of the administrative decisions that I have to make. I am vested with certain authority and I exercise that authority, I hope, to the satisfaction of Hon. Members.

to be consulted in an all-Party sense when it comes to changing the heritage nature of these buildings.

subsubtopic: MR. DOMM-ALLEGED UNPARLIAMENTARY LANGUAGE OF MR. LAPIERRE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to draw your attention and the attention of the House to a comment made on page 24889 of Hansard by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Lapierre). Immediately following my discussion dealing with the important question of bilingualism, the Parliamentary Secretary had the audacity to refer to me as "frog basher" and accuses me personally of "francophobia" as well as "rancoeur" as applied to bilingualism.
This scurrilous remark by a Member of Parliament is not only disgraceful, it is a malicious act quite unbecoming a Member of Parliament, and if far from the truth of the reported record in Hansard. The Parliamentary Secretary's statement is in itself an unwarranted and contemptuous act. It smacks of prejudice, discrimination, and very much of bias. It is quite demeaning and disgraceful not only with respect to me personally but to all French Canadians as well.
In fact, the Parliamentary Secretary's slanderous comments seriously damage the reputation of this entire institution and, as such, I would like to draw your attention to a recent case involving the Hon. Member for Lincoln (Mr. Mackasey) who stated on page 23834 of Hansard:
Madam Speaker, these false and slanderous accusations ... tarnished my reputation and, if left unchallenged, could even blemish the reputation of this institution and those who serve in it; for as I noted just two weeks ago in debate, the reputation of the House reflects the individual and collective integrity of its Members.
As the Hon. Member for Lincoln also stated:
The privileges of this House, of its Members, are privileges which have been accumulated through the centuries, privileges which we guard jealously in this House.

subsubtopic: IMPACT OF INTEREST RATES ON GOVERNMENT DEFICIT
speechtext:
1.	Is the Economic Council of Canada's econometric model capable of estimating the impact on short-term and long-term interest rates in Canada for varying levels of the Government deficit and (a) if not, for what reason (b) if so, what change in short-term and long-term interest rates from current levels does it predict if the deficit were (i) 0 (ii) $10 billion (iii) $20 billion?
2.	What impact would the changes in interest rates have on the cost of servicing the national debt?

speakeroldname: Mr. David Smith (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: IMPACT OF INTEREST RATES ON GOVERNMENT DEFICIT
speechtext:
1. Yes. (a) Not applicable, (b) (i), (ii) and (iii) Precise changes in short-term and long-term interest rates from current levels cannot be predicted unless the way in which the deficit is to be reduced to the specified levels is also indicated by the questioner. In general, however, lower deficits would influence interest rates downward.
2. The direct effect is clearly positive; that is, changes in interest rates lead to changes in debt servicing costs, in the same direction, given no change in the Government debt portfolio.
Indirect effects of interest rate changes on national debt servicing costs can also occur. For example, rising interest rates may lead to decreased economic growth which, in the absence of policy change, would reduce Government revenues and increase Government expenditures, thereby raising the level of the stock of Government debt or changing the composition of the Government debt portfolio toward higher yield debt instruments. This would also increase the cost of servicing the debt.
A full response to the question would require consideration of the causes of changes in interest rates, over-all economic responses to these changes, and Government policy and program reaction to both the direct and indirect effects of interest rate changes.

speechtext: The House is in the situation where questions, answers and comments might be addressed with respect to the remarks of the Hon. Member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle). subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset I would like to express my pleasure in participating in this budget debate. More important than that, I would like to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) for producing a budget document which focuses primarily on the creation of jobs and the reduction in unemployment.
It is becoming increasingly clear, Mr. Speaker, that in order to meet the competition in the 1980s and beyond, Canadians are questioning actively whether we need to reorganize ourselves. We feel, unless we improve our competitive position, that Canada could slide into third rate power status and our standard of living drop.
To respond to this challenge the Government has a responsibility to set the tone and to foster a climate of co-operation with business and labour in a way acceptable to both Parties and consistent with the national interest.
This is one of the reasons why, prior to bringing down the budget, the Minister of Finance and other Cabinet Ministers embarked upon an intensive round of discussions with so many people. Mr. Speaker, I want to focus most of my remarks on the labour discussions. We listened carefully to labour's concerns and responded to their suggestions with initiatives designed to improve labour's role. Let me give you some examples.
Labour called for stimulative spending, encouragement of economic growth, extended Unemployment Insurance and increases in public investment. The budget did not and, under the current circumstances of restraint, could not deliver all that labour, or indeed any other group wanted. But the $4.8 billion recovery program announced in the budget goes a long way to meeting their concerns. Let us look at what the Government has done in reply.
Labour proposed long-term low interest loans for home ownership. They argued that individuals should be permitted to withdraw up to $2,000 tax free from their RHOSPs, and recommended a broad reduction of taxes for low and middle income earners.
The Budget-Mr. Caccia
Recognizing the recent fall in interest rates that has rendered less pressing labour's demand for lower interest rates, the Government focused its efforts on specific stimulation. Five existing housing programs were expanded and extended by the addition of $120 million to the Canadian Home Renovation Plan, $40 million to the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program, $40 million for Indian-on-Reserve Housing, and $30 million to the Canadian Home Ownership Stimulation Plan. The 1983 allocation for social housing units was established at the original level of 25,000 units. The Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan has been strengthened so as to allow withdrawals to purchase furnishings, appliances, and new homes. Until the end of 1984, individuals can deduct from taxable income, in one lump sum, up to $10,000 for the purchase of a new home.
Labour recommended a broad reduction of taxes. Low and middle income earners will benefit from several tax concessions. In addition to the RHOSP amendments, the restructured child benefit package doubles the child care expense deduction from $1,000 to $2,000 per child and from $4,000 to $8,000 per family. Low income earners also benefit from more generous employment expense deductions which have been increased from 3 per cent to 20 per cent of employment income up to $500 per employee.
Labour made a number of recommendations for the encouragement of economic growth including, for example, the expansion of research and development and measures to improve productivity.
The Special Recovery Program expands budgets for research and development, and encourages the application and use of high technology. Specifically, $290 million will be spent on research facilities, $180 million is allocated for high technology procurement, $100 million has been earmarked for new technology initiatives, and as well, proposed tax incentives worth $185 million are contained in the budget paper, "Tax Policies for R and D". These are responses to labour's suggestions.
Labour groups in the pre-budget consultations argued for measures to ease some of the impacts of the recession. Some of these recommendations included the continuation of benefits to those who have exhausted their Unemployed Insurance, a moratorium on foreclosures and a stabilization of mortgage rates, the improvement of retirement income, and a continuation of the work-sharing program. In reply, the Government will expand the NEED Program and Section 38 of the Unemployment Insurance Act. In addition, $2.4 billion will be spent on the new Capital Projects Program. These programs, coupled with the construction incentives, should create jobs and ease the level of unemployment. New tax treatment of business losses and increased access to investment tax credits and the refundable investment tax credit should go a long way in assisting farmers and small business out of their financial difficulties. All of these measures will help to create more jobs.

April 28, 1983
The Budget-Mr. Caccia
Many specific initiatives that labour proposed are addressed by the $2.4 billion Special Recovery Capital Projects. The new projects will include transportation as one of six key areas and could include assets needed for resource development, including expanded reforestation efforts. The Special Recovery Capital Project Board announced in the budget will seek the co-operation of management, labour and the Provinces in implementing such projects.
Why this examination, you may ask, of what labour has proposed and what has been included in the budget? Why this comparison between what has been suggested and what has been accepted? Because it is important for labour to know that it has been listened to, that it has had an influence on the shaping of the budget. Many of the major items proposed by labour have won the recognition of the Government. Why is it important to establish this fact? At a time when mistrust and cynicism seem to prevail in society, trust is needed more than ever. Trust it like cement. It bonds lasting relationships. Without trust, a society is doomed to fall apart. With trust, it can face difficulties with confidence and build the institutions it needs for a better future.
In the April, 1983 budget the Government has responded positively to the proposals received from labour. The essence of the labour proposals is threaded through the budget with its focus on economic recovery. There is abundant evidence for labour to conclude that the Government, because of its budget performance, can be trusted. We hope that this trust will lay the grounds for a new coalition of interests which will search energetically for solutions to our industrial problems.
For workers and their organizations, the stakes are high. As new technologies take hold, unions risk becoming participants in a struggle between present workers seeking to retain a shrinking number of jobs in existing companies and the employment expectations of younger applicants seeking a first job.
Recently unions in Canada and the United States have begun, consciously, to adapt themselves to the kind of future I have tried to describe. The report from the communication workers of America's Committee on the Future is a calm, tough-minded and remarkably lucid proposal for a union which faces both changes and opportunities in a newly deregulated industry. In appealing to the union's members, the committee asked:
Are we going to let ourselves be overtaken by explosive social and technological change? Are we going to let ourselves be stuck with obsolete skills, competing against younger workers who are better trained for new-era jobs? Are we going to let ourselves just be swept along with the information age tide?
It would be easy for any organization to give pro forma and ritual answers to these questions. It will be hard to address real changes in collective and individual attitudes.
For all the difficulties, I am unrepentantly confident that we can make those changes in business, in labour and in Government. We cannot congratulate ourselves on the state of labour management relations in Canada, nor can we bury past
experience, without which we would be children indeed. Fortunately, we are not compelled forever to wage old battles. It is in the future we are fated to live. We alone will be responsible for its shape. We designed a budget with these considerations in mind. It is intended to set a course for improved and extended co-operation between labour and management and all Canadians.
The budget contains a proposal to establish a national centre to focus on the areas of employment growth, technology and productivity. This follows up on one of the main recommend-tions contained in the Labour Canada task report on microelectronics and employment, entitled "In The Chips: Opportunities, People and Partnerships". It was released last November.
When we speak of a centre for employment growth, technology and productivity, we speak of an institution which requires trust in order to get off the ground, an institution which could provide a vehicle for consultation and co-operation, one which could provide practical advice and direction on managing technological change, one which could help to educate business, labour and other interested parties about these problems, and one which could find ways to increase jobs and improve the human aspects of employment.
Furthermore, we speak of an institution which may, for instance, assist workers and management to develop and implement new methods of co-operative management in their place of work, one which may acquire and disseminate information on technological change, productivity improvements, co-operative management methods, training methods and related methods, and one which may sponsor training courses for workers and managers related to the centre's objectives. We speak of an institution from which labour could derive immense benefits.
Labour has a major role to play in shaping Canada's technological future, a role it already plays by participating in Hamilton at the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety, and in Ottawa, at the Labour Adjustment Benefits Board, at the Textile Advisory Board and at the Export Development Board.
We know that for the national centre for technology, productivity and employment growth to get off the ground, it will require consultations with all the partners together, to establish terms of reference, structure and mandate. Therefore, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Lumley) and I will begin consultations to seek common ground on the makeup and mission of such a centre.
The success of these consultations is crucial. Workers often fear, from experience, that they could be excluded from key decisions and they might be expected to bear the bitter costs of job displacement and outmoding of hard-earned skills learned over the years and employment-related stress. As consumers, working Canadians will be the beneficiaries of change, but as workers, they see themselves, more often than not, as victims. Microelectronic innovations are seen to liberate workers, not
April 28, 1983

just from drudgery but also from their jobs. Electronic monitoring can offer the employer a fool-proof check on individual performance and productivity. In an adversarial system, innovation can become the ally of one side and the enemy of the other. The inevitable outcome is a struggle which workers cannot win and Canada cannot afford.
Every example from our experience shows that Canadians are a future-minded, adaptive people, yet we are also a humane people with a profound sense of justice. Among our saving virtues is a commitment to social solidarity and an equal rejection of the devil-take-the-hindmost philosophy or the equally repelling notion of class warfare. The Government believes that the fruits of improved productivity must be distributed fairly and must not be won at the expense of workers but, rather, in co-operation with them.
Because of the history of their development, neither business nor labour in Canada have developed structures or traditions which make consultation easy. At the plant and shop level, it is true that the bargaining unit gives Canadian workers a basis for industrial democracy which is largely missing from the European structure. In some industries, there is a matching of labour and employer organizations, which has helped make our sectoral task forces a preliminary model for the kind of effective co-operation we are seeking.
What we are proposing now is a further evolution in our means of securing an effective degree of co-operation among all sectors. This is why we have proposed a centre for the practical consideration of employment growth and of technological and productivity issues. If all the potential partners in this venture have the determination to tackle, with open minds, the difficult problems facing us, we will be equal to the task of ensuring Canadians a future they can manage.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question to the Minister relates to his remark that in the budget his Government had responded positively to labour. The Minister must know, along with other Canadians, that the budget is in fact a supply side document, which means that the financial elbow room which the Government has had has been turned over to the private sector in the hope that jobs will eventually result. However, when we are in the middle of the recession, there is no way that that will result in increased jobs. In fact, labour has called for immediate stimulus of consumer spending and for direct job creation by way of public works. What I am wondering is how the Minister can say that the Government has responded positively in the budget to labour when, in fact, he has adopted a supply side economic budget rather than one which stimulates the economy and consumer spending.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot blame the Hon. Member, perhaps, for not having listened carefully to what I had said. I had to move quickly because of the limitation of time. He should know that in the budget there is a provision of $2.4 billion in the Special Recovery Capital Projects. Perhaps he does not realize that. Perhaps he does not realize that in the budget there is a provision for $120 million for the Canadian
The Budget-Mr. Caccia
Home Renovation Program. There is a provision of $40 million for residential rehabilitation assistance programs, provision of $40 million for housing for Indians on reserves, and $30 million for the Canadian Home Ownership Stimulation Plan.
The measures which are embodied in the Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan, those which come into effect between now and the end of the year, and the other measure coming into effect between now and the end of 1984, are stimulative measures. Therefore, I find it unbelievable that the Hon. Member would ask such a question, revealing such ignorance about the content of the budget, which he evidently has not taken the trouble to read, to study and to analyse. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out to the Minister that the budget increases personal income tax and therefore takes money out of the pockets of Canadians.
